    A self-paced tutorial and 90-minute hands-on workshop

    Turn the materials you already have into slides Building, illustrating, and checking presentation decks with AI

    You have readings, notes, and old decks. AI tools can turn them into a draft presentation in minutes. This page shows you how in five tools, then spends real time on the parts AI does poorly: visuals that teach, slides everyone can use, and facts you can stand behind.

    Before you start

    • Have an account for at least one tool covered here: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, or Gamma. Free accounts work for most of the session; What AI does with slides notes where a paid plan helps.
    • Pick 1–3 files on one topic: a reading, your lecture notes, or an old deck you'd like to rebuild. A single unit works better than a whole course.
    • Use only material you have the right to upload. Never upload student names, work, or grades.
    • If you have a department or college PowerPoint template, bring a copy.
    Facilitator: Each demo uses a different section of the same source; see the demo prep checklist in Lab 1. This page assumes PHYS 106 Module 1, Our Place in the Universe (seasons, Moon phases, eclipses), which is openly licensed and visual. Save a finished deck from each tool in case a live demo stalls. Keep the "seasons are caused by distance from the Sun" misconception in mind: AI drafts sometimes repeat it, which makes a good accuracy moment in Lab 3.

    What AI does with slides

    0:05 – 0:12

    AI is fast at structure and first drafts. You're still responsible for whether the deck teaches well and says true things.

    Good at

    Turning a long reading into a slide outline, splitting a dense slide into several, rewriting for a different audience, suggesting visuals, and matching an existing template.

    Needs your judgment

    Choosing what students should actually learn, deciding the order of ideas, and picking examples that fit your students.

    Often wrong

    Confident factual errors, made-up citations, images that look right but aren't, text in images, and alt text that describes appearance instead of meaning.

    Two kinds of tools

    Every tool in this workshop falls into one of two families. Knowing which one you're using tells you where the deck lives and what you'll get at the end.

    Inside PowerPoint

    An add-in opens a side panel in PowerPoint. The AI builds and edits real, editable slides in your file, and can follow your template's fonts, colors, and layouts.

    Claude for PowerPoint, ChatGPT for PowerPoint, Copilot in PowerPoint

    Best when you already have a template or an old deck to revise.

    Generate, then export

    You work in the AI tool's own window, then export to PowerPoint, Google Slides, or PDF and finish editing there.

    Gemini Canvas, Gemini Notebook, Gamma, Claude chat

    Best when you're starting from a reading or notes and want a designed first draft quickly.

    Your account situation

    Select the one that matches your school.

    Your school uses Microsoft 365

    • You probably have PowerPoint already, so the "inside PowerPoint" family fits naturally. Claude and ChatGPT add-ins sign in with your own Claude or ChatGPT account, not your school account.
    • Add-ins may be blocked. Some schools turn off the Office Store for employees. If you can't find or install an add-in, ask IT, or use a web tool and download the .pptx.
    • Gemini and Gemini Notebook need a Google account. Use a free personal one. To get a PowerPoint file, export to Google Slides, then download as .pptx.
    • Check your AI policy before using outside tools for course work, and keep uploads to material you could post publicly.

    Your school uses Google Workspace for Education

    • Gemini with your school account is covered by your school's Google agreement, and Canvas decks export straight to Google Slides.
    • Your admin decides which Gemini features are on. If Canvas or export is missing, contact IT.
    • PowerPoint add-ins need PowerPoint (desktop or web) and your own Claude or ChatGPT account.

    Using personal accounts

    • Every tool here offers a free tier. Free limits run out quickly in a workshop, so plan which drafts matter.
    • Personal accounts aren't covered by your school's data agreements. Upload only your own or openly licensed material.
    • Read each tool's privacy settings. Some let you opt out of having your content used to improve their models.

    The core workflow

    0:12 – 0:20

    Five steps that work the same way in every tool.

    1. Gather your sources. Upload the reading, notes, or old deck. The AI's draft is only as good as what you give it, and sources let you check its claims.
    2. Get an outline first. Ask for slide titles and one line per slide, then edit the outline before any slides exist. Fixing the story here takes seconds; fixing it in finished slides takes much longer.
    3. Draft the deck. Generate slides from your approved outline, in your template if you have one.
    4. Make it visual. Replace bullet lists with diagrams, tables, charts, or images where they teach better (Lab 2).
    5. Check it. Verify facts against your sources, run an accessibility pass, and add speaker notes (Lab 3).

    Decide what the deck is for

    A deck you'll talk over and a deck students read on their own are different things. Tell the AI which one you want.

    Presenter deck

    Short titles, few words, strong visuals. The explanation lives in your voice and the speaker notes.

    Read-alone deck

    Full sentences and more detail, because no one is there to explain. Often better posted as a document or PDF.

    Build an outline prompt

    Fill in the fields, copy the prompt, and paste it into your tool with your files attached.

    In Gamma, paste this into Generate and edit the outline it shows. In the other tools, read the outline in chat, ask for changes, then say "Build the slides from this outline."

    Lab 1: Build a deck from your files

    0:20 – 0:45

    Lab 1 has two parts. First, five short demos (about 10 minutes) show each tool doing the job it does best. Then you pick one tool and build your own deck (15 minutes), using the step-by-step tab for that tool below.

    The demos

    Every demo uses the same source, Module 1 of an open astronomy textbook (PHYS 106: Our Place in the Universe), so you can compare the tools fairly. Each one covers a different part of the module and highlights a different strength. The first three start from a reading; the last two revise a deck that already exists.

    Demo 1: Gamma

    2 minutesStarting from a reading

    Shows: fixing the story in an outline before any slides exist, then a designed deck in under a minute.

    Input: the module's section on seasons, pasted in as text.

    Prompt
    Make an 8-slide presenter deck on why Earth has seasons for first-year college students. One idea per slide.

    Watch for: the outline editor (reordering and deleting cards), theme choice, and the watermark on a free export.

    Demo 2: Gemini Canvas

    2 minutesStarting from a reading

    Shows: a themed deck with images, revised by prompt and sent to Google Slides.

    Input: the module's section on Moon phases, uploaded as a PDF.

    Prompt
    Create a 6-slide presentation explaining Moon phases for first-year students, using only the attached file. Then: replace slide 3 with a diagram of the Moon's positions.

    Watch for: the images Gemini chose (are they accurate?), the theme you didn't pick, and Export to Slides.

    Demo 3: Gemini Notebook

    1 minuteStarting from several sources

    Shows: a deck grounded in a whole notebook of sources, revised one slide at a time.

    Input: a notebook built ahead of time with the full module plus one related reading, and a Presenter slides deck already generated.

    Prompt (on one slide)
    Simplify this slide to three short points and add a labeled diagram.

    Watch for: click into the downloaded PowerPoint. The text can't be selected because each slide is an image. That comes back in Lab 3.

    Demo 4: Claude for PowerPoint

    2 minutesRevising an existing deck

    Shows: new slides built inside your own template, as real editable PowerPoint objects.

    Input: an old, text-heavy deck on eclipses, open in the Brookdale PowerPoint template.

    Prompt
    Rebuild slides 2 through 4 in this template. Keep my content, one idea per slide, and turn the solar versus lunar eclipse slide into a two-column comparison.

    Watch for: the template's fonts and colors carried over, and clicking into the new comparison table to edit it. Mention the chat route for free accounts.

    Demo 5: ChatGPT for PowerPoint

    2 minutesRevising an existing deck

    Shows: AI as a reviewer: finding weak slides and anticipating student questions, with your approval before each change.

    Input: the same eclipse deck, after Demo 4.

    Prompt
    Which slides in this deck would be hardest for first-year students to follow, and what questions will they ask? Then fix the hardest slide.

    Watch for: the confirmation step before ChatGPT changes a slide.

Before the session: save the seasons section as text and the Moon phases section as a PDF; build the Gemini Notebook notebook and generate its deck (it can take a few minutes); prepare an old, text-heavy eclipse deck in the college template; sign in to all five tools in separate browser tabs, with both PowerPoint add-ins installed.     Claude

    Claude can make slides two main ways. Use chat if you're on a free plan; use the add-in if you have a paid plan and a template.

    Option A: In chat (any plan)

    1. At claude.ai, open Settings and make sure file creation (code execution) is turned on.
    2. Start a new chat, attach your source files, and paste your outline prompt.
    3. Edit the outline in conversation until the story is right.
    4. Ask: "Build these slides as a PowerPoint file." Claude creates a .pptx you can preview and download.
    5. To change one slide, name it: "On slide 4, replace the bullets with a two-column comparison."

    Option B: Claude for PowerPoint (paid plans)

    1. Install Claude for PowerPoint from the Microsoft Marketplace (select Get it now).
    2. Open PowerPoint (desktop or web), open your template or old deck, then open the add-in: Home > Add-ins on Windows or Tools > Add-ins on a Mac. Sign in with your Claude account.
    3. Apply your template first. Claude reads its slide master, fonts, and colors and uses them for new slides.
    4. Paste your outline prompt in the side panel, or ask it to rebuild the deck you have open.
    5. Target specific slides when revising. Claude warns you before overwriting existing content.

    Claude Design (claude.ai/design) is a third option for visually designed decks. It is in research preview, so features and availability may change.

    ChatGPT for PowerPoint

    An add-in that works inside PowerPoint, available on free ChatGPT accounts as a beta.

    1. In PowerPoint, find ChatGPT for PowerPoint in the Microsoft Marketplace (or the add-ins menu) and install it.
    2. Open the add-in and sign in with your ChatGPT account.
    3. Open your template or old deck, then paste your outline prompt in the side panel. Ask for the outline before the slides.
    4. Review each change. ChatGPT asks you to confirm before larger edits.
    5. Ask it about the deck itself: "Which slides are hardest to follow, and what questions will students ask?"

    Without PowerPoint, you can attach files in a ChatGPT chat and ask for a downloadable .pptx. The design is usually plainer than the add-in's.

    Gemini Canvas

    Builds a themed deck with images in the Gemini app, then exports it to Google Slides.

    1. Go to gemini.google.com and sign in. Select Tools, then Canvas.
    2. Attach your source file and paste your outline prompt. Ask for the outline in chat first.
    3. Ask Gemini to create the presentation. The deck appears in the Canvas panel beside the chat.
    4. Revise by prompt: "Replace slide 3 with a timeline."
    5. Select Share & export, then Export to Slides. Finish editing in Google Slides.
    6. Need PowerPoint? In Google Slides, choose File > Download > Microsoft PowerPoint (.pptx).

    Canvas chooses its own theme. Apply your template in Google Slides after export.

    Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM)

    The tool from Workshop 1. Its Slide Deck draws only on the sources in your notebook, so it's strongest when a deck has to pull together several readings accurately. If you already built a notebook in Workshop 1, start there.

    1. Go to notebook.google.com and open a notebook, or create one and add your sources.
    2. In the Sources panel, check only the sources this deck should cover.
    3. In the Studio panel, select the pencil icon on Slide Deck. Choose Presenter slides to talk over or Detailed deck to read on its own.
    4. Paste the middle part of your outline prompt (audience, focus, number of slides) into the prompt box and generate. There's no separate outline step, so be specific here.
    5. To change a slide, type the change in that slide's prompt box, then generate the revised deck.
    6. From the three-dot menu, download as PDF or PowerPoint.

    Know the trade-off

    Gemini Notebook draws each slide as a single image. Even the PowerPoint download has one picture per slide, so you can't fix a typo by clicking it, and screen readers can't read the slide text. It's excellent for drafting content and planning a deck. For anything you'll post to students, either rebuild the deck in an editable tool (paste the slide text into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gamma) or add alt text to every slide that includes all of its text.

    Gamma

    A dedicated presentation tool with polished designs and an outline editor built in.

    1. Go to gamma.app and sign up (free).
    2. Choose Create new, then Paste in text or Import a file to start from your material. Use Generate to start from a prompt instead.
    3. Set the card count and review the outline Gamma proposes. Edit, reorder, or delete cards before generating.
    4. Pick a theme and generate.
    5. Revise with the AI editor or by hand.
    6. Select Export and choose PowerPoint, PDF, or PNG.

    Free credits are one-time, not monthly, and free exports include a watermark. Gamma uses cards rather than fixed slides, so expect some layout cleanup after a PowerPoint export.

    At a Microsoft school: Copilot in PowerPoint

    Microsoft's own Copilot can create and edit slides inside PowerPoint. Some features now work with the free Copilot Chat that comes with many school accounts, while others, such as creating a presentation from a file, may need an additional license. Open PowerPoint, look for the Copilot button on the Home tab, and ask IT what your account includes.

    Hands-on lab: draft a deck

    About 15 minutes, after the demos.

    Lab 2: Visual aids and diagrams

    0:45 – 1:05

    Most AI drafts are walls of bullets. Your job is to find the slides where a picture would teach better.

    Not every slide needs a visual. Add one when it shows something words can't: a sequence, a comparison, a trend, or a physical arrangement.

    Match the visual to the content

    Choose what's on the slide to see what to make and a prompt to try.

    Choose a content type.

    Editable shapes beat pictures of shapes

    Ask for diagrams and charts as native PowerPoint or Slides objects whenever you can. You can fix a wrong label in an editable diagram in seconds, screen readers can read its text, and it stays sharp at any size. A generated image of a diagram is a flat picture: misspellings and wrong arrows are baked in.

    Editable visuals compared with generated images
    Editable diagram or chartGenerated image
    Fix a labelClick and typeRegenerate or edit in an image editor
    Screen readersCan read the textNeed alt text
    Best forProcesses, comparisons, charts, timelinesScenes, illustrations, title or mood images
    Most reliable inPowerPoint add-ins, then exportsGemini, Gamma, and image tools

    Build a visual prompt

    Need an original illustration?

    For images and infographics, use the Graphics Prompt Studio from Workshop 2. It builds detailed image prompts for any discipline that you can paste into ChatGPT or Gemini, then insert the result into your deck.

    Check every visual

    • Read every label and arrow. Diagrams can look right and be wrong.
    • Check chart numbers against your source data.
    • Zoom in on generated images for garbled text, extra fingers, or impossible objects.
    • Use images you have rights to. Generated images and stock from the tool are usually fine; images pulled from the web may not be.

    Hands-on lab: make three slides visual

    About 15 minutes, using the deck from Lab 1.

    Facilitator: Demo the Moon phases slide from Module 1: bullets first, then an editable diagram, then a generated image. Point out any label errors in the image version; there usually is one.

    Lab 3: Accessibility and revision

    1:05 – 1:17

    A slide that some students can't read, hear, or follow isn't finished.

    AI tools rarely check accessibility on their own, and many colleges now expect posted course materials to meet accessibility standards such as WCAG 2.1 AA. Check your institution's policy. The habits below cover most of what matters.

    Unique slide titles

    Every slide gets a real, different title. Screen reader users navigate by them.

    Meaningful alt text

    Describe what an image teaches, not just what it looks like. Mark decorative images as decorative.

    Not color alone

    Pair color with labels, patterns, or text so meaning survives for colorblind viewers and grayscale printouts.

    Contrast and size

    Dark text on a light background (or the reverse) and fonts large enough to read from the back of the room.

    Reading order

    Screen readers read objects in the order they were added, which may not match how the slide looks. Check it.

    Less per slide

    One idea per slide. Split dense slides instead of shrinking the text.

    Audit this slide

    This slide came from an AI draft. Check every problem you find, then select Check my audit.

    Slide 4

    • Earth's seasons are caused mainly by Earth being closer to the Sun in summer and farther away in winter.
    • Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5 degrees relative to its orbit.
    • The tilt changes how directly sunlight strikes each hemisphere.
    • Direct sunlight spreads energy over a smaller area.
    • Day length also changes over the year.
    • The hemispheres have opposite seasons.
    • As you can see in the image, the summer and winter positions differ.
    IMG_2041.jpg
    Summer Winter
    Which problems does this slide have?

    Your results appear here.

    Use the built-in checkers

    • PowerPoint: select Review > Check Accessibility. It flags missing alt text, missing or duplicate slide titles, low contrast, and reading order problems, and helps you fix each one.
    • Google Slides: add alt text by right-clicking an image and choosing Alt text. Slides doesn't include a full checker like PowerPoint's, so check titles, contrast, and order by hand, or download as .pptx and run PowerPoint's checker.
    • Image-based slides: decks from Gemini Notebook (and any slide pasted in as a picture) have no real text. Checkers can't see the problem, so add full alt text yourself or rebuild the slides as editable text.
    • Ask the AI to audit: both PowerPoint add-ins can review the open deck. Use the prompt below, then fix and verify each item yourself.
    Accessibility audit
    Review this deck for accessibility. For each slide, check: a unique, descriptive title; alt text that explains what each image teaches; meaning that doesn't depend on color alone; enough contrast; and no more than one main idea. List problems by slide number with a suggested fix, but don't change anything until I approve.

    Hands-on lab: check and fix your deck

    About 8 minutes.

    Speaker notes

    1:17 – 1:22

    Good speaker notes keep slides light, help you present, and give students a text version of what you said. Posting a deck with notes is a quick way to support students who missed class or use a screen reader.

    • Ask for notes in your voice: talking points and examples, not a script to read word for word.
    • Ask for timing cues and where to pause for questions.
    • Edit the notes. AI tends to repeat the slide text instead of adding to it.
    Write speaker notes
    Write speaker notes for each slide. Use short talking points, not a script. Add what the slide doesn't say: one example, one common student mistake, and a question I can ask the class. Keep each slide's notes under 100 words and use only my sources.
    Notes as a transcript
    Rewrite the speaker notes as full sentences so a student who missed class could read them alongside the slides and understand the lesson.

    Sharing and responsible use

    1:22 – 1:25

    Getting the deck out

    Export formats by tool
    ToolBest exportOther options
    Claude.pptx (chat) or your own PowerPoint file (add-in)Open the .pptx in Google Slides or Keynote
    ChatGPTYour own PowerPoint file (add-in)A .pptx download from chat
    GeminiGoogle SlidesPDF; .pptx by downloading from Google Slides
    Gemini NotebookPDFPowerPoint (one image per slide), or share the notebook
    GammaPDF, or a shareable web linkPowerPoint, PNG

    For students, post a PDF or the editable file in your LMS. PDFs keep the layout; editable files keep alt text and speaker notes most reliably. Check that alt text survived the export.

    Responsible use

    Check accuracy

    AI drafts can state common misconceptions with confidence. Verify every claim you present.

    Protect privacy

    Don't upload student names, work, or grades, especially on personal accounts.

    Respect copyright

    Upload material you own or can openly use, and check the rights on any image you didn't generate.

    Be transparent

    Tell students when AI helped make course materials and how you reviewed them.

    Keep it accessible

    Run the checker before every post, not just the first.

    Keep your voice

    Edit generic phrasing so the deck sounds like you and fits your students.

    Knowledge check

    1:25 – 1:30

    Ten questions. You get feedback as soon as you choose an answer.

    Quick reference

    Take-away
    Glossary

    Add-in: a tool that runs inside PowerPoint in a side panel.

    Slide master (template): the fonts, colors, and layouts a deck is built on.

    Native or editable object: a chart, diagram, or text box you can change directly in PowerPoint or Slides.

    Alt text: a text description of an image for people using screen readers.

    Reading order: the order a screen reader reads the objects on a slide.

    Presenter deck: slides designed to be talked over.

    Read-alone deck: slides designed to be studied without a presenter.

    Outline-first: approving slide titles and order before generating slides.

    Credits: the usage units some tools, such as Gamma, charge for AI actions.

    Troubleshooting

    I can't find the add-in. Your school may block the Office Store. Ask IT, or use a web tool and download the .pptx.

    The new slides ignored my template. Apply the template before generating, and start from a deck that uses it.

    My export looks different. Fonts and layouts can shift between tools. Check every slide after export, and expect cleanup from Gamma's card layouts.

    Every slide is a wall of text. Ask for a presenter deck, set a word limit per slide, and split dense slides.

    A generated image has garbled text. Ask for the image with no text, then add labels as editable text boxes.

    Gemini won't export to Slides. On a school account, your admin may have turned export off. Try PDF, or a personal account with non-sensitive material.

    I can't edit the text in my Gemini Notebook deck. Its slides are images. Revise with the per-slide prompts, or copy the content into an editable tool.

    My Gamma export has a watermark. That's the free plan. Paid plans remove it.

    I ran out of free uses. Limits reset over time on most tools; Gamma's free credits don't. Save your best prompts so retries count.
